title: Stock counts: tablets left, supply for N days, ampoules or nebules needed
blurb: Work out tablets used, tablets left, how long a supply lasts and how many ampoules to open, rounding up where you must.
question: A client has 112 tablets of sodium valproate 200 mg in stock and is prescribed 400 mg twice a day. How many tablets will be left after 7 days?

teach.body: Formal rule: tablets left = stock − (tablets per dose × doses per day × days). Plain English: find how many tablets one dose uses, how many a whole day uses, then how many the period uses, and take that from the stock. Supply questions turn it round: days a supply lasts = stock ÷ tablets per day. Stock and nebule counts appeared on the midwifery practice paper.
teach.cite: FACTS.md section 4 (stock remaining, ampoules needed); Pearson VUE NMC midwifery practice paper

teach.h: Worked example: Kieran in supported living
teach.body: Kieran Walsh, 34, has 112 tablets of sodium valproate 200 mg and is prescribed 400 mg twice a day. Tablets per dose = 400 ÷ 200 = 2. Per day = 2 × 2 = 4. For 7 days = 4 × 7 = 28 used. Left = 112 − 28 = 84 tablets. Sense-check: 84 ÷ 4 = 21 more days of supply.

teach.text: Counting doses instead of tablets: when each dose is two tablets, "twice a day for 7 days" uses 28 tablets, not 14. A second trap is answering with the tablets used when the question asks how many are left.

teach.caption: You cannot open part of an ampoule. The unused part is discarded per local policy.

teach.h: Worked example: ampoules on a birth unit
teach.body: Precious, a midwife, has a prescription for 125 mg of a medicine IM. Each ampoule contains 100 mg. 125 ÷ 100 = 1.25, so she opens 2 ampoules, draws up the 125 mg and discards the rest. Rounding down to 1 ampoule would give only 100 mg.

items: Tablets used = per dose × doses per day × days.
Days a supply lasts = stock ÷ tablets per day.
Ampoules or nebules to open: divide, then round UP to a whole number.
Traps: counting doses not tablets; giving tablets used when asked for tablets left.

summary: You can now calculate tablets needed, tablets left and how long a supply lasts, always counting tablets rather than doses. You can also work out how many ampoules or nebules to open, rounding up when the dose is not a whole number of them.

A.q: A service user has 56 tablets of olanzapine 5 mg in stock and is prescribed olanzapine 10 mg once a day. How many tablets will be left after 7 days?
A.why: Per dose = 10 ÷ 5 = 2 tablets. Used in 7 days = 2 × 7 = 14. Left = 56 − 14 = 42 tablets.

whyNot.0: Counted one tablet a day (doses) instead of two tablets.
whyNot.2: This is the number used, not the number left.
whyNot.3: Treated once a day as twice a day.

A.q: A woman is prescribed salbutamol 5 mg nebulised four times a day. Each nebule contains salbutamol 2.5 mg. How many nebules are needed for 24 hours?
A.why: Per dose = 5 ÷ 2.5 = 2 nebules. Four doses: 2 × 4 = 8 nebules.

whyNot.0: Counted one nebule per dose instead of two.
whyNot.1: This is the number for one dose.
whyNot.2: Used six doses instead of four.

A.q: A client is supplied with 60 tablets and is prescribed 2 tablets twice a day. How many days will the supply last?

whyNot.1: Divided by tablets per dose, not tablets per day.
whyNot.3: Counted 8 tablets a day, doubling the daily use.

B.q: A woman is prescribed 75 mg of a medicine by intramuscular injection. The ampoules available contain 50 mg each. How many ampoules must be opened?
B.why: 75 ÷ 50 = 1.5 ampoules. You cannot open half an ampoule, so round up: 2 ampoules.

whyNot.0: 1.5 is the share of drug needed, but ampoules are opened whole.
whyNot.3: Divided by 25 mg instead of the 50 mg in each ampoule.

B.q: A person is to be discharged with a 14-day supply of risperidone 3 mg twice a day. The tablets available contain risperidone 1 mg each. How many tablets are needed?
B.why: Per dose = 3 tablets. Per day = 3 × 2 = 6. For 14 days = 6 × 14 = 84 tablets.

whyNot.1: Counted once a day instead of twice.
whyNot.2: Counted doses (one tablet each) instead of three tablets per dose.

B.q: A client has 100 tablets of levetiracetam 500 mg in stock and is prescribed levetiracetam 1 g twice a day. How many tablets will be left after 10 days?
B.why: 1 g = 1000 mg, so per dose = 1000 ÷ 500 = 2 tablets. Per day = 4. Used in 10 days = 40. Left = 100 − 40 = 60 tablets.

whyNot.1: This is the number used, not left.
whyNot.2: Used four doses a day instead of two.

C.q: A woman has 90 tablets of a medicine 210 mg and is prescribed 420 mg twice a day. How many tablets will be left after 14 days?
C.why: Per dose = 420 ÷ 210 = 2 tablets. Per day = 4. Used in 14 days = 56. Left = 90 − 56 = 34 tablets.

whyNot.2: This is the number used, not left.

C.q: A service user is supplied with 84 tablets of a medicine 500 micrograms and is prescribed 1 mg twice a day. How many days will the supply last?
C.why: 1 mg = 1000 micrograms, so per dose = 2 tablets. Per day = 4 tablets. Days = 84 ÷ 4 = 21 days.

whyNot.0: Counted one tablet per dose (2 a day).

C.q: A woman is prescribed 30 mg of a medicine by intramuscular injection every 6 hours. Each ampoule contains 20 mg, and each dose is drawn up from newly opened ampoules. How many ampoules are needed for 24 hours?
C.why: Per dose: 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5, so open 2 ampoules. Every 6 hours = 4 doses. Total = 2 × 4 = 8 ampoules.

whyNot.1: Divided the daily total (120 mg) by 20 mg, as if part ampoules carried over between doses.
whyNot.2: This is the number for one dose.
whyNot.3: Rounded each dose down to one ampoule.

reteach.title: Tablets per day first
reteach.question: Each dose is 2 tablets, twice a day. How many tablets does one day use?

blocks.body: Per dose 2 tablets. Twice a day: 2 × 2 = 4 tablets per day. For a week: 4 × 7 = 28. Every stock sum is built on the tablets-per-day figure.

blocks.text: Read the final question: "how many left" and "how many needed" are different answers from the same working.

explain.body: Tablets needed = tablets per dose × doses per day × days.

test.q: A person is prescribed 2 tablets three times a day. How many tablets are needed for 7 days?

whyNot.1: Used twice a day instead of three times.

test.q: A client has 28 tablets in stock and takes 2 tablets each morning. How many tablets will be left after 5 days?

whyNot.2: This is the number used, not left.

explain.body: Days = stock ÷ tablets per day. One tablet three times a day is 3 tablets a day.

test.q: A person has 120 tablets and is prescribed one tablet three times a day. How many days will the supply last?
A person is prescribed 600 micrograms of a medicine by injection. Each ampoule contains 0.5 mg. How many ampoules must be opened?
test.why: 0.5 mg = 500 micrograms. 600 ÷ 500 = 1.2, so round up: 2 ampoules.

whyNot.1: Rounded 1.2 down: one ampoule gives only 500 micrograms.
whyNot.2: Ampoules are opened whole: round up.
whyNot.3: 0.5 mg was taken as 50 micrograms, giving 12.
